company: Bombay Coated and Special Steels Limited

summary.one_line: BCSSL is a fast-growing but thin-margin steel service centre that slits and cuts JSW coated coils for AC and refrigerator makers. The ₹183 cr all-fresh issue mostly repays bank debt rather than funding growth. With 85% of coil purchases from one supplier under an agreement that expires in March 2027, promoter-family loans at 12%, and a long list of late RoC filings, this is one to track, not to buy at the IPO.
bull_points: Revenue from operations grew from ₹755.3 cr in FY24 to ₹1,266.8 cr in FY26, a 29.5% CAGR. Q1 FY27 revenue was ₹397.1 cr (S2, p.235; S3).
The issue is 100% fresh with no OFS. ₹125 cr goes to repaying bank borrowings and ₹15.77 cr to buying out leased Ghiloth equipment, so all proceeds stay in the company (S2, p.117-122).
Leverage has fallen steadily: debt/equity was 4.31x in FY24, 3.33x in FY25, 2.78x in FY26 and 2.00x in June 2026 (S2, p.242).
The customer list includes Amber Enterprises, Western Refrigeration, Haier, Dixon, PG Technoplast and EPack. 98% of Q1 FY27 revenue came from existing customers (S2, p.35, p.246).
The auditor reported no qualifications for any restated period, and there is no outstanding litigation by or against the company or its promoters (S3).
bear_points: 85-91% of steel coil purchases came from a single supplier, JSW Steel Coated Products, between FY24 and Q1 FY27. The service-partner agreement runs only to 31 March 2027, is non-exclusive, and JSW can terminate it on three months' notice (S2, p.31-32, p.284).
Margins are thin and shrinking: PAT margin was 2.80% in FY24, 2.72% in FY25 and 2.41% in FY26. FY26 PAT grew only 6.5% on 20% revenue growth (S2, p.242, p.446).
Cash conversion is weak. Cumulative operating cash flow over FY24-FY26 was ₹53.8 cr against cumulative PAT of ₹80.3 cr, while investing outflows were ₹129.6 cr (S3).
Promoter-family members have lent ₹19.5 cr to the company at 12%, against bank lines at 7.55-9%. This debt is not being repaid from the IPO (S2, p.464-465).
The RHP lists 26 delayed RoC filings over five years and a mis-filed share allotment for which an adjudication application is still pending (S2, p.32-33).
watch_points: Whether JSW renews the service-partner agreement beyond 31 March 2027, and on what terms (S2, p.284).
Whether working-capital debt is drawn back up after the IPO repayment. Borrowings rose from ₹273.7 cr in June 2026 to ₹302.4 cr by 31 August 2026 (S2, p.119, p.407).
Use of the new promoter pay ceilings, which allow up to ₹10 cr a year for the three executive directors against FY26 pay of ₹0.66 cr (S2, p.290; S15).
Day-1 subscription data was not yet published at the time of writing. Only the anchor book (₹54.10 cr) is known (S8).

reasoning: The money raised improves the balance sheet but does not build the business. 89% of the earmarked net proceeds (₹125 cr of ₹140.77 cr) repays bank loans, mostly yearly-renewable working-capital lines, and ₹15.77 cr buys out machines already in use. No capacity is added. The Ghiloth expansion is funded separately from accruals and borrowings (S2, p.117-122, p.250). The lower interest bill is real, but the business needs working capital, and the lines being repaid can be redrawn.

There is no real moat. BCSSL is a non-exclusive authorised service partner of JSW, which can appoint competitors in the same regions or expand its own processing. Annual PAT margins of 2.4-2.8% are consistent with a commodity-processing intermediary that has little pricing power. Q1 FY27's 3.8% falls in the peak AC season and should not be annualised (S2, p.31, p.235-236; S14).

Two relationships carry the business: one supplier (85.13% of Q1 FY27 coil purchases) and the appliance cycle (89.93% of Q1 revenue from home and commercial appliances). The top customer, Amber, alone was 19.97% of revenue. The supplier contract's expiry in March 2027 falls inside the first year of listing (S3; S2, p.35, p.284).

Governance is acceptable but loose. Seven promoter-family parties (five individuals and two HUFs) lend to the company at 12%, above any bank line. The company leases its Bhiwandi plant and an office from promoters. Pay ceilings were raised about 15-fold just before the IPO. There are 26 late RoC filings and a pending adjudication over the 2021 business-transfer allotment (S2, p.32-33, p.285, p.290, p.465).

Growth is real but low quality. Revenue compounded at 29.5% from FY24 to FY26, while PAT grew 20% a year and operating cash flow lagged profit in FY24 and FY26. FY24 profit was also boosted by other income worth 36% of PBT. One or two listed quarters would show whether the post-IPO margin and cash flow hold up (S2, p.235, p.443; S3).

blocks.text: BCSSL is a steel processing centre (SPC). It buys wide steel coils, mostly coated coils (galvanised, colour-coated, galvalume) plus some hot- and cold-rolled coils, and turns them into slit coils, cut-to-length blanks, embossed slit coils and blanks, and sheared blanks to each customer's dimensions. It sits between the steel mill and the appliance or engineering manufacturer. It also holds inventory and delivers just in time, typically keeping about one to one-and-a-half months of a customer's requirement in stock (S2, p.239, p.253, p.259).

The business is a re-incorporation of an older family trade. Promoter Vijaykumar Gupta began trading steel as the proprietorship M/s Bombay Steels in 1983 and moved into processing with the Bhiwandi unit in 2012. The current company was incorporated in December 2019 and bought Bombay Steels as a going concern under a business transfer agreement dated 29 January 2021, for ₹87.61 million. That consideration was settled with 24,50,000 shares and ₹63.11 million credited to the promoter's loan account (S2, p.239, p.283).

Revenue is product sales priced off the input coil plus a processing and logistics margin. The company reports a single operating segment, 'processing of steel coils'. Raw material dominates the cost base: materials consumed were 87.6% of total income in FY26 and 83.05% in Q1 FY27. Material costs plus other operating costs leave very little margin (S3; S2, p.443).

blocks.caption: Revenue by end-use industry (₹ million, % of revenue from operations)
rows: General engineering total (auto, electrical, ventilation etc.)

blocks.text: The business has become more concentrated, not less. Appliances rose from 77% of revenue in FY24 to 90% in Q1 FY27, and general engineering shrank in absolute terms from FY25 to FY26. This runs against the RHP's stated strategy of diversifying the end-user base (S3; S2, p.249).

BCSSL runs four plants on 42,209 sq m in total: Wada (Palghar) and Bhiwandi (Thane) in Maharashtra, Ghiloth (Alwar, Rajasthan, on the Delhi-Jaipur highway) and Sri City (Andhra Pradesh, near Chennai). Each sits close to appliance clusters. It also has a warehouse at Dera Bassi, Punjab. Plant machinery comes from suppliers in South Korea, Turkey and China (S2, p.240, p.246-248).

blocks.caption: Revenue by facility (₹ million, % of revenue)

blocks.text: Total installed capacity rose from 301,541 MTPA in FY24 to 350,411 MTPA in FY25 and 462,411 MTPA in FY26, a 23.83% CAGR (S2, p.250). Utilisation has not kept pace. In FY26, slitting ran at 60.61%, cut-to-length at 58.74%, embossing at 46.68% and shearing at 59.86%. In Q1 FY27 slitting ran at 63.84% and embossing at 30.49% (S3). Volume growth is coming from new lines, not from fuller plants, and that capacity adds depreciation, which rose 46% in FY26 (S2, p.446).

The RHP's capacity figures are not internally consistent. It gives aggregate capacity 'as of June 30, 2026' as 1,23,153 MTPA, which is a quarterly figure. One passage calls that number the slitting capacity alone. The industry report shows Ghiloth at 2,47,000 MTPA and Sri City at 33,852 MTPA (S2, p.230, p.248, p.250). These are disclosure-quality issues rather than red flags, but readers should use the annual FY26 figure of 462,411 MTPA.

Inputs come mainly from JSW Steel Coated Products and its holding company (JSWSCPL), for which BCSSL has been an authorised service partner since 2021. JSW supplied 84.58% of coil purchases in FY24, 90.61% in FY25, 86.65% in FY26 and 85.13% in Q1 FY27 (₹2,397.74 million of ₹2,816.64 million). JSW also supplies technical support and quality-control protocols (S2, p.243-244).

blocks.caption: Customer concentration (% of revenue from operations)

blocks.text: The largest customer was Amber Enterprises in FY25, FY26 and Q1 FY27 (₹2,584.60 million, or 20.40%, in FY26) and Western Refrigeration in FY24. Other named top-10 customers in FY26 were Western Refrigeration (15.98%), Haier Appliances (8.70%), PG Technoplast (5.84%), Dixon Electro (3.46%) and EPack Durable (1.76%). Four of the top ten are not named because they did not consent (S2, p.35). Several of these are contract manufacturers (ODMs), which made up 55.92% of FY26 revenue (S3).

The RHP describes long-standing customer relationships, yet it also says relationships with 'several of our top 10 customers' range from about one-and-a-half to just over three years as of June 2026 (S2, p.246). Most of the customer book is young.

According to the company-commissioned CareEdge report, the Indian steel processing centre industry grew at an 8.6% CAGR from CY20 to reach USD 8.2 billion in CY25, and is projected to reach USD 12.4 billion by CY30 at 8.6% a year (S3; S2, p.252). By service, cut-to-length was USD 1,707 million in CY25, slitting USD 1,501 million and blanking USD 892 million. Projected CY26-30 growth for these is 6.8-7.4% (S2, p.241).

End markets matter more than the SPC market for BCSSL because 90% of its revenue is appliances. CareEdge projects the Indian air-conditioner market growing at a 15% CAGR to ₹936.1 billion by CY29 and water heaters at 11.3% to ₹350.1 billion (S2, p.250). The report also cites the 2025 GST cut on ACs from 28% to 18% as a demand tailwind (S2, p.226).
All market figures come from an industry report the company commissioned and paid for, as the RHP itself discloses (S2, p.239). They are directionally useful but not independent.

The RHP's peer set contains three listed companies: BMW Industries, Manaksia Coated Metals & Industries, and Shiv Aum Steels. The report profiles end-users such as Voltas, Daikin, Haier, V-Guard and LG rather than rival SPCs (S2, p.230-235). Real competition also includes other JSW service partners, steel mills' own processing arms, and in-house slitting by large OEMs. The RHP says JSW is free to appoint additional service partners in BCSSL's regions and to expand its own processing facilities (S2, p.31).

blocks.caption: Operating comparison with RHP peers, FY26 (excludes valuation metrics)

blocks.text: BCSSL has grown fastest in this set but has the highest leverage, and its PAT margin is below the peer median of 3.52% (S2, p.235-236). Its high reported ROE (29.92% in FY26) mainly reflects a small equity base funded by debt, not superior margins.

Not a meaningful one. The RHP's 'high entry barriers' amount to the capital needed for slitting and cut-to-length lines, OEM vendor qualification, and proximity to customer plants (S2, p.248-249). These raise the cost of entry somewhat but are the same for every regional service centre. BCSSL makes no import-substitution claim, no market-share claim and no 'only Indian maker' claim, and holds no proprietary technology (S2, p.230-249).

items: The JSW relationship is the main asset, and BCSSL does not control it. The agreement is non-exclusive, runs to 31 March 2027, can be ended by JSW on three months' notice, and restricts BCSSL from buying the same coated products from other mills (S2, p.31-32, p.284).
Plant location near Amber, Western Refrigeration, PG Technoplast and EPack plants is a genuine service advantage, but it can be copied (S2, p.240).
OEM approvals create some switching friction, but customer turnover is high: 75 of 261 FY26 customers were new (S2, p.246).

blocks.text: Bottom line: BCSSL is a well-run regional intermediary that depends on a supplier's goodwill and a customer group's cycle. There is no structural moat that would protect margins if JSW changed terms or appointed another partner nearby.

Source for the table: S2, p.242 and p.443, and S3. Revenue grew 39.8% in FY25 and 20.0% in FY26. Management attributes this to new capacity, Sri City ramping up, and more business from both existing and new customers (S2, p.445-447). Profit grew more slowly. FY26 PAT rose only 6.5% because finance costs (+14%), depreciation (+46%) and employee costs (+48%) all grew faster than revenue (S2, p.445-446).

Earnings quality needs adjusting. In FY24, other income of ₹101.53 million (including ₹63.94 million of subsidy) was 36% of PBT. Stripping it out, PBT was ₹180.5 million in FY24, ₹342.3 million in FY25 and ₹377.8 million in FY26 (analyst calculation from S2, p.443, p.447). Underlying growth is therefore strong from FY24 to FY25 but only about 10% in FY26. EBIT covers interest only about 2.1x in each year (₹764.97 million EBIT vs ₹357.08 million finance cost in FY26; S2, p.242, p.443).

Q1 FY27's 3.8% PAT margin and 8.1% EBITDA margin cover April-June, the peak season for AC components. The RHP itself says appliance orders are seasonally weaker from June to September (S2, p.249). Do not annualise this quarter.

Source for the table: S2, p.437, p.440, p.449-450, and S3. Equity growth was funded by retained profit, a 3:1 bonus issue in July 2025, and a preferential allotment of 900,091 shares at ₹88 in October 2025 that raised about ₹79 million (S2, p.405). Leverage improved mainly because equity grew. Absolute debt rose every year to March 2026.

The June 2026 fall in debt is partly a timing effect. Borrowings fell by ₹647.6 million in the quarter because inventory was run down by ₹638.7 million (S2, p.449). By 31 August 2026, total outstanding borrowings had risen back to ₹3,024.28 million, including about ₹301 million of new five-year term loans from Kotak, IndusInd, RBL and Bank of Baroda taken in June-July 2026 (S2, p.463-464). Working capital stayed tight throughout: the current ratio was 0.93-1.10 and net working capital ran 58-70 days (S3; S2, p.439).
No defaults, restructurings or covenant breaches are disclosed, and the auditor reported no qualifications (S2, p.283, p.434, p.440). The balance sheet is stretched but not distressed.

From FY24 to FY26, operating cash flow totalled ₹537.9 million against cumulative PAT of ₹803.5 million, about 67% conversion. Capex and other investing outflows of ₹1,296.4 million were funded with debt and the ₹79 million equity raise (analyst calculation from S3). The RHP lists negative investing and financing cash flows as risk factor no. 3 (S2, p.34).

The strong ₹723 million operating cash flow in Q1 FY27 came largely from releasing inventory built up at March 2026 (inventory fell from ₹1,893.27 million to ₹1,254.60 million). It is a one-off swing, not a new level of cash generation (S2, p.449).

Verdict on the trend: revenue growth is real and capacity-driven, but margins, cash conversion and interest cover have not improved with scale. The growth story the IPO is selling needs margin expansion that the history does not yet show.

blocks.text: Filing history: the DRHP was first filed with SEBI on 1 October 2025 (S4; S16). A revised DRHP was filed on 30 January 2026 (S5). SEBI issued observations on 12 June 2026 (S17), and the RHP is dated 21 October 2026 (S1). Promoters and the promoter group are not participating in the issue (S2, p.115).
Because there is no OFS, every rupee raised goes to the company. The promoters are not cashing out at the IPO.

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds (₹ million)
rows: Buy-out of capital equipment under Siemens Financial Services leases

blocks.text: Source for the table: S2, p.117-118 and p.123. Some brokers show GCP as ₹42.29 cr (S12). That figure is gross proceeds minus the two named objects and ignores issue expenses, so actual GCP will be lower.

The Siemens buy-out covers four machines installed at Ghiloth in 2024: a high-speed slitting line, a narrow cut-to-length line, an embossing line and two EOT cranes, originally costing ₹219.97 million. The balance payable is ₹157.70 million. Buying them out removes a lease expense of ₹46.86 million a year (FY26) but adds no capacity (S2, p.121-122; S14).

blocks.caption: Borrowings identified for repayment, outstanding at 31 Aug 2026 (₹ million)

blocks.text: Source for the table: S2, p.120. About ₹1,569 million of the ₹1,811 million eligible is working-capital lines renewable every year. Only ₹242 million is term debt. Repaying working-capital lines lowers interest immediately, but the business needs inventory and receivables funding, so those lines can be redrawn. On our rough estimate, ₹1,250 million at an average rate of about 8% saves around ₹100 million a year in pre-tax interest (analyst estimate from S2, p.120). Measured against FY26 PBT of ₹407.88 million (S2, p.443), that is meaningful.

The ₹195.07 million of 12% loans from promoter-family members is not among the loans being repaid. The RHP also bars GCP from repaying promoter or director loans (S2, p.118, p.465). The costliest debt therefore stays on the books while cheaper bank debt is retired.

There are three promoters, all from one family. Vijaykumar Himatrai Gupta (Chairman and Whole-time Director) studied to class 9, has more than 40 years in steel trading, and founded Bombay Steels in 1983. His son Nitin Vijaykumar Gupta (Managing Director, B.Com 2001, about 20 years in steel) holds 78.22% pre-issue and runs day-to-day operations. Nitin's wife, Bhawna Nitin Gupta (Whole-time Director, B.Com Hons 2001), has six years in the industry (S3; S2, p.288-289). The promoters run no other group companies, subsidiaries or JVs (S2, p.283).

The board has six members: three family executives and three independent directors, all appointed on 21 March 2025 in the run-up to the IPO. Neelam Tater (35) is a CA. Mihen Halani (38) is a practising company secretary. Hemant Ostwal (46) is a CA/CS and SEBI-registered research analyst, previously with RR Kabel, Bajaj Corp and Videocon D2H (S2, p.287-289). Key managerial personnel are CEO Shashi Mohan Singh Rawat, CFO Ashish O Sonthalia and Company Secretary Sonam Gupta. The previous CFO, Lokesh Lavti, left on 31 August 2025 (S3; S2, p.399). We did not verify the CEO's and CFO's prior careers in the RHP.

items: Before the IPO, promoter pay was ₹6.6 million in FY26: ₹3.0 million for Nitin and ₹1.8 million each for Vijaykumar and Bhawna (S2, p.399; S15).

New ceilings effective 26 September 2026 allow up to ₹60 million a year for Nitin and ₹20 million each for the other two, plus variable pay. Together that is up to ₹100 million, against FY26 PAT of ₹305.39 million (S2, p.290).
Independent directors receive a ₹30,000 sitting fee per meeting (S2, p.290).

blocks.text: The related-party section is not routine. No promoter-linked business sits on the customer or supplier side, but the family acts as both lender and landlord. Seven related parties (Nitin, Vijaykumar, Bhawna, Sunita and Ruchi Gupta, and two HUFs) had lent the company ₹195.07 million at 31 August 2026. These are business loans repayable on demand at 12% (S2, p.465). The company also borrowed ₹9 million at 12% from two outside entities, Maharashtra Rolling India and Shree Salasar Ferro Metal (S2, p.465).
Source for the table: S2, p.399 Note 40, with rows summed by the analyst. Leases from promoters (S2, p.285; S15):

items: Bhiwandi plant (Nitin Gupta): 60 months from 1 January 2026 at ₹80,000 a month.
Vile Parle office (Vijaykumar and Sunita Gupta): ₹50,000 a month. The RHP says the office is used only occasionally for meetings.

blocks.text: The family loans cost 12%, roughly 3-4 points above the company's 7.55-9% bank lines (S2, p.120, p.465), and are not being repaid from the issue. The amounts are small relative to revenue, but they move about ₹25-30 million a year of interest to the controlling family. The promoters also give personal guarantees and pledge residential property for the bank loans (S2, p.465), which lowers the company's borrowing cost but deepens its dependence on the family.

The RHP's second risk factor discloses statutory-filing lapses. When the company allotted 24,50,000 shares to Vijaykumar Gupta under the 2021 business-transfer agreement, it did not file Form MGT-14 and mislabelled the allotment as a 'rights issue' on Form PAS-3. It has since filed corrections and an adjudication application dated 6 January 2026, which is still pending before the RoC. A separate application of 13 May 2026 to mark the original PAS-3 as defective is also pending (S2, p.32).

The same risk factor lists 26 forms filed late with additional fees over five years, mostly charge-creation forms (CHG-1), auditor and cost-auditor appointments, a deposits return, and preferential-issue forms. The most recent is a CHG-1 due in late 2025 and filed on 9 April 2026 (S2, p.32-33). No penalties have been imposed so far.

items: Outstanding litigation is nil for the company, the promoters and the KMPs. The only item is a ₹0.58 million income-tax demand and penalty against independent director Hemant Ostwal for AY 2019-20 (S3).
Pre-IPO equity: a 3:1 bonus issue in July 2025, and 900,091 shares allotted on 28 October 2025 at ₹88 to outside investors, including Moneyplant SME Fund, which holds 113,637 shares (S2, p.405; S3).

The RHP contains small internal inconsistencies. Note 2.27 says there are no borrowings secured on current assets, while Note 41(c) says working-capital limits are sanctioned against current assets. Capacity and plant start dates also differ between sections (S2, p.400, p.436).

blocks.text: Overall governance read: there is no fraud or litigation red flag, but this is a tightly family-run company whose secretarial discipline has been weak until very recently, and whose board independence is only 19 months old.

items: 1. Supplier dependence and contract expiry. 85.13% of Q1 FY27 coil purchases came from JSWSCPL. The agreement is non-exclusive, expires 31 March 2027, can be terminated on three months' notice or for any act JSW deems prejudicial, and includes minimum-purchase commitments and limits on sourcing coated steel elsewhere (S2, p.30-32, p.284).

2. End-market and customer concentration. AC and refrigeration were 88.4% of Q1 FY27 revenue, the top 10 customers 73.54% and Amber alone 19.97%. A weak summer or a large ODM switching processors would hit volumes directly (S3; S2, p.35).

3. Thin margins under steel-price and leverage pressure. PAT margin is 2.4-2.8% a year, and materials are about 88% of income. A small fall in processing spread or an inventory loss on a steel-price drop could erase most of the profit (S2, p.443; S3).

4. Working-capital-heavy growth. FY24-26 operating cash flow was only about two-thirds of PAT, and debt rebuilt to ₹3,024 million by August 2026 after the Q1 paydown. Without better cash conversion, the IPO deleveraging could reverse (S3; S2, p.463).

5. Under-used capacity. Utilisation is about 59-61% on the main lines (embossing 30% in Q1), yet the company plans another cut-to-length line at Ghiloth on land bought for ₹116.87 million. Extra fixed costs without volume would squeeze margins further (S3; S2, p.250).
6. Governance and compliance. There is a pending RoC adjudication, 26 late filings, 12% promoter loans and pay ceilings up to ₹100 million (S2, p.32-33, p.290, p.465).
7. Industry data comes only from a paid report. The market-size and peer figures are from a company-commissioned CareEdge report (S2, p.239).

blocks.text: Generic risks such as Indian macro conditions, listing-price volatility and US securities restrictions are left out on purpose. They apply to every IPO and do not change this decision.

Three developments would materially de-risk the story. First, a multi-year JSW renewal or a second mill partnership. Second, FY27 operating cash flow at or above PAT, with bank debt staying near post-IPO levels. Third, repayment of the 12% family loans after listing. None of these is promised in the RHP.

blocks.text: The JSW agreement expires before the end of BCSSL's first full year as a listed company. Investors are effectively betting on a renewal that is entirely at a third party's discretion.

The only forward-looking statements we found are the strategies the board approved on 24 September 2026 and set out in the RHP (S2, p.249-253). We found no management interview, analyst call or quantified guidance in any searched source (S2; S16; S17).

items: Diversify away from seasonal AC and refrigeration demand into water heaters, washing machines and automotive (S2, p.249-250).

Expand Ghiloth by one cut-to-length line on an adjoining 11,250 sq m plot bought on 29 September 2025 for ₹116.87 million, funded from accruals and borrowings. No cost estimate or completion date is given (S2, p.250).
Improve the debt profile through the IPO repayment (S2, p.251).
Grow geographically and in exports. Exports were nil in FY26 and Q1 FY27, and Bangladesh was ₹10.22 million in FY24 (S2, p.251-252).
Cut costs through scale, yield, automation and owning rather than leasing equipment (S2, p.253).

blocks.text: The financial statements say there were no material post-balance-sheet events (S2, p.400). The capital-work-in-progress of ₹69.94 million at June 2026 is all under one year old, and none of it is overdue or over budget (S2, p.400).

The strategy is plausible but generic, and it is not quantified. The diversification goal is contradicted by recent history: the appliance share rose from 77% to 90% between FY24 and Q1 FY27 (S3). The Ghiloth expansion adds capacity to a network running at about 60% utilisation (S3). The cleanest near-term earnings lever is lower interest after the IPO repayment plus the removed Siemens lease expense of ₹46.86 million (S2, p.122). That should lift reported PAT in FY27-28 even without operating improvement.
Beyond the strategy list, management has not said anything concrete about growth targets, margins or capex budgets. Any revenue projection would be our extrapolation, not company guidance.

subsections.title: Anchor book, day-1 status and grey market

blocks.text: On 28 October 2026, BCSSL raised ₹54.10 crore from anchor investors by allotting 65,97,500 shares at ₹82. That is 29.55% of the issue (S8; S7). Half of the anchor shares (32,98,750) are locked in for 30 days and half for 90 days (S8). Brokers give the tentative lock-in end dates as about 2 December 2026 and 31 January 2027 (S12).

blocks.caption: Anchor allocation
rows: IMAP India Capital Investment Trust - Catalyst New India Fund

blocks.text: Source for the table: S8. Every anchor is an AIF (₹40.02 cr) or an NBFC (₹14.08 cr). There are no domestic mutual funds, insurers or FPIs in the book (S7; S8), so the anchor list is not a strong institutional endorsement.

The issue opened on 29 October 2026, the day this report was written. At research time, Chittorgarh showed no subscription data yet (S8) and Investorgain's live page had not posted category figures (S11). No retail, NII or QIB subscription numbers exist yet, and nothing here should be read as a demand signal.

The grey market premium is unofficial and inconsistent. Investorgain shows ₹9 as of 29 October, up from ₹0 on 22 October (S9), while another tracker showed ₹0 (S10). GMP is unregulated dealer chatter, not a reason to apply, and it played no part in our verdict.

method: Primary sources were the full 594-page RHP dated 21 October 2026, downloaded from the BRLM's offer-documents page (S6), and SEBI's abridged prospectus. I read these sections directly: risk factors, capital structure, objects of the issue, industry peer comparison, our business, history and material agreements, our management, restated financial statements including the Note 40 related-party table, other financial information, MD&A results discussion, and financial indebtedness. Page numbers cited are printed RHP page numbers. Issue terms, anchor allocation, GMP and filing history were cross-checked against Chittorgarh, Zerodha, Groww, Investorgain, Chanakya Ni Pothi, Multibagg, PTI and Angel One, and against the SEBI filing pages. Figures marked as analyst calculations (family-loan totals, underlying PBT excluding other income, cumulative cash conversion, interest-saving estimate) are derived arithmetically from RHP tables. Gaps: (1) I did not read the RHP's Our Promoters chapter or the detailed KMP biographies, so the CEO's and CFO's prior careers are unverified. (2) The full Industry Overview narrative was only partly read (peer comparison and threats sections). (3) Issue expenses, and therefore exact GCP, are blank in the RHP. (4) No retail, NII or QIB subscription data had been published when this report was written on opening day. (5) No management interview or call was found, so the outlook relies only on the RHP's strategy section. Valuation multiples were deliberately excluded.
